steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that presents new families of topological subsystem codes built from semi-regular tessellations. It should give the historical background from early quantum computing through quantum error correction to subsystem codes and earlier topological subsystem code constructions, and then outline the sections of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Early quantum computing models
- Decoherence and quantum error-correcting codes
- First quantum codes, CSS and stabilizer codes
- Topological codes (toric code)
- Subsystem codes and topological subsystem codes
- Structure of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline

- Topological codes
  - next year: Kitaev's toric code, class of topological codes
  - stabilizer generators act on few qubits in neighborhood -> geometrically local
  - makes quantum words resistant to local noise
- Subsystem codes
  - part of stabilizer codes
  - stabilizer formalism applied to operator quantum error correction
  - generalizes standard theory; unified framework: active correction + passive error prevention; very versatile class
- Topological subsystem codes
  - Bombín: construction with trivalent, 3-colorable tessellations
  - another work used tessellations earlier, but non-local stabilizer generators -> not topological
  - Suchara, Bravyi, Terhal: conditions; generalization of Kitaev's honeycomb model for trivalent hypergraphs; necessary and sufficient condition for measuring error syndrome -> guarantees code is topological
  - Sarvepalli and Brown: new construction inspired by that, new code families; one of few works giving code parameters (hard to determine certain standards)
- Structure
  - Sec 2: review subsystem codes, groups needed for construction/definition
  - Sec 3: topological subsystem codes, advantages vs topological quantum codes; constructions of Bombín and generalizations; two families from Sarvepalli and Brown
  - Sec 4: new hypergraph \Gamma_{h}, proof it allows subsystem codes; stabilizers and other data
  - Sec 5: four families: two from \Gamma_{h}, one from Sarvepalli-Brown construction (case not addressed), one from tessellation \{p,3,4,3\}; proof they are topological; parameter tables

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The first quantum computing model was described in 1982 by Benioff. It was based on quantum kinematics and dynamics, but in the computational sense established in another work it was effectively classical. Also in 1982, Feynman proposed the first computer model that was based on the principles of quantum mechanics, and this model was the closest thing to a universal quantum simulator. Already in 1985 there was a major breakthrough in this area, when Deutsch described an entirely quantum model of a quantum version of the Turing machine.

One of the biggest difficulties in doing quantum computing is quantum decoherence, which is the issue of quantum decay, and Unruh warned about it. One way to get around this effect is to use quantum error-correcting codes. These are mathematical tools that are used to encode the physical states of a quantum system.

The first quantum error-correcting codes were inspired by classical error-correcting codes, which were introduced in 1948 by Shannon. In 1995, Shor introduced the first quantum error-correcting code. It was a combination of two other three-qubit codes. One of them protects the quantum state against bit flip errors and the other one protects it against phase-flip errors, and only the first one has a classical analog.

In 1996 there was one of the biggest advances in quantum coding, which was the construction of the CSS quantum codes by Calderbank and Shor and Steane. From these codes came one of the most important classes of quantum codes known to date, the stabilizer quantum codes.

The year after, Kitaev developed a new code, Kitaev's toric code, which belongs to a class of codes called topological codes. A big advantage and novelty of this code was that its stabilizer generators acted on a small number of qubits in its neighborhood. Codes with this property are called geometrically local. The advantage of stabilizer generators acting on a small number of qubits in their neighborhood is that it makes quantum words resistant to local noise.

Another important group of quantum codes, which are also part of the stabilizer codes, are the subsystem codes,,. These codes come from applying the stabilizer formalism to quantum error correction of the operator,. This generalizes the standard theory of quantum error correction and gives a unified framework for active error correction and passive error prevention techniques, so subsystem codes are one of the most versatile classes of quantum error-correcting codes.

Many works have been done in this area over the years. A big step was the construction of topological subsystem codes by Bombín, which used trivalent and 3-colorable tessellations. Tessellations had already been used to construct subsystem codes in another work, but the stabilizer generators of those codes are non-local, so they cannot be considered topological.

Suchara, Bravyi, and Terhal gave some conditions for determining topological subsystem codes, and they proved that topological subsystem codes can be seen as a kind of generalization of Kitaev's honeycomb model for trivalent hypergraphs. Also in the same work they presented a necessary and sufficient condition for measuring the error syndrome of a subsystem code. This is a very important result, and it is used to guarantee that a subsystem code is topological.

Sarvepalli and Brown presented a new construction of topological subsystem codes inspired by that work, and they presented some new code families. This is one of the few works where code parameters are given, because it is difficult to determine certain standards in this class of codes.

The work is organised as follows. In Section 2 we review subsystem codes and present their main elements, like the groups that are needed for their construction and definition. In Section 3 we discuss topological subsystem codes, including some important advantages they have compared to topological quantum codes. We also cover the main aspects of the construction of these codes in the work of Bombín and their generalization in the work of Suchara, Bravyi, and Terhal and the work of Sarvepalli and Brown. Then we look at two families of topological subsystem codes presented in their work. In Section 4 we construct a new hypergraph \Gamma_{h} and prove that it allows the construction of subsystem codes. We also present in general some stabilizers and other relevant data about this construction. In Section 5 we present four families of topological subsystem codes. Two of these families come from particular cases of the hypergraph \Gamma_{h} from Section 4. The third family comes from the construction given in the work of Sarvepalli and Brown, but from a case the authors did not address, and the fourth family comes from a hypergraph built from the tessellation \{p,3,4,3\} in a similar way as the previous families. In this section we also prove that these code families are topological subsystem codes and give some tables with parameters.
